I have two Java services on our Solace event broker. When a rider requests a trip, a BookingService asks a FareQuoteService for the current fare estimate and waits for the answer before showing it. The quote service computes it in memory and replies immediately. This is a fast synchronous lookup; if no answer comes back quickly the booking flow just retries or shows a default, and nothing about the exchange needs to be persisted. How should I structure this ask-and-wait messaging between the two services?

My team is putting together a payments platform where two Java services communicate through our Solace event broker. A PaymentGateway submits a settlement request to a LedgerService and needs the confirmation for that specific request back (a settlement ID and the amount posted). This is a committed transaction, so neither the request nor the confirmation can be lost, and if the LedgerService happens to be restarting when the request arrives it must still process it and reply once it's back up. How should I structure this request-and-reply so both the request and the reply are reliable?

We're working on a plant-monitoring system where two Java services talk through our Solace event broker. A TelemetryPublisher pushes temperature and vibration readings from the factory floor several times a second, and a LiveDashboard service consumes them to redraw a wallboard. If a few readings get dropped it makes no difference since the next one supersedes them, and there's no reason to store any of this. Volume is high and I care about low latency, not durability. How should I structure the messaging between these two services?

In the banking system I'm developing, two Java services communicate through our Solace event broker. A TransactionPoster publishes ledger entries that adjust account balances, and a BalanceProjection service consumes them to maintain the authoritative balance. These entries must not be lost if the projection service goes down, and they must be applied strictly in the order they were published because each one depends on the previous balance. I want exactly one instance processing at a time, with a standby that takes over in order if the active one fails. How should I structure the messaging to guarantee this?

Our order-fulfillment system runs two Java services connected through our Solace event broker. An OrderIntake service emits a PickPackJob for every confirmed order, and these jobs absolutely cannot be lost. A FulfillmentWorker handles them, but at peak one instance can't keep up, so I want to run several identical copies of the worker and have any free worker pick up the next job. Ordering between jobs doesn't matter to me; throughput does. How should I structure the messaging so I can scale the workers out without losing any jobs?

For the logistics platform we run in Java on our Solace event broker, a ShipmentTracker service publishes a DeliveryException event whenever a package misses its checkpoint. Three separate services each need to act on it independently: a CustomerNotifier emails the customer, a ReroutePlanner recalculates the route, and an AnalyticsIngest service records it for reporting. Each is owned by a different team, each needs its own full copy of every event, and none of them can miss one even if that service is down for maintenance. How should I structure the messaging so every one of these services reliably receives every event on its own?
